subtype: Stage 4: Peak and point of no return [Actor]
passage:
Sunday: Ankita and Jyoti argued over the rent for their PG room, again. Jyoti was always a few days late, and Ankita was sick of reminding.
Monday: It boiled over. "Maybe if you'd cleared your exam the first time, you'd have a real job and could pay on time," Ankita said. The room went silent. Jyoti's face flushed deep red, and the answer came back: "At least my parents still talk to me." Both of them froze. Ankita felt her stomach drop; she knew she'd hit the failed exam on purpose. But she crossed her arms and said nothing, and so did Jyoti.
Wednesday: They still hadn't spoken. Each had typed "sorry" twice and deleted it.

qa.q: What were Ankita and Jyoti arguing over on Sunday?
qa.a: They argued over the rent for their PG room.

qa.q: What did Ankita feel right after the remark about the exam?
qa.a: Her stomach dropped; she knew she had hit the failed exam on purpose, yet pride kept her arms crossed and her mouth shut.

qa.q: What could still be done at this point of no return?
qa.a: One of them could send the deleted "sorry" and name the exact remark, such as "The exam comment was cruel, I take it back."

qa.q: What is Jyoti likely experiencing after the remark about the exam?
qa.a: Jyoti probably feels shame and anger at once, which is why the reply about parents came so fast and cut so deep.

grounding: Shows a cruel remark hitting a known sore spot, both friends flashing with shame and anger, and pride stopping either from taking it back.

subtype: Stage 4: Peak and point of no return [Actor]
passage: Ayesha, sit down, drink your tea. You're angry with your roommate, I can see it. Let me tell you something. When I was twenty, in the nursing hostel in Kochi, I had a best friend called Leelamma. We argued over a borrowed saree she had stained. It got hotter and hotter, and then I said it: "No wonder your father left, look how careless you are." I saw her face go white. My own face burned with shame the same second. I knew I had gone too far. Still, I was proud, and she was angry, and I walked out instead of taking it back. We didn't speak for two years. I'm Kavitha, fifty-four years old, and I still remember her face. Don't let one sentence cost you two years.

qa.a: She had stained a borrowed saree.

qa.q: What did Kavitha feel the moment the remark about the father came out?
qa.a: Kavitha felt shame burn at once and knew it was too far, but pride made walking out easier than taking it back.

qa.q: What is Kavitha hoping Ayesha will do differently?
qa.a: Kavitha hopes Ayesha will take back a cruel sentence quickly instead of letting pride cost years of friendship.

qa.q: How did Leelamma likely experience that remark?
qa.a: Leelamma was hit on a deep sore spot about her father; her face going white shows the shock and hurt.

grounding: Shows a young woman's remark striking a friend's family wound, the instant shame and anger, and pride blocking an apology.
